You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Nineveh

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, Nineveh functions primarily as the great symbol of repentance and of God's mercy extended even to the most wicked of pagan peoples. The city that repented at Jonah's preaching becomes the paradigm of a sinful people turning to God and being spared, and Jesus himself invokes the 'men of Nineveh' as exemplars of repentance who will condemn an unrepentant generation. Closely bound up with this is Nineveh's role as a sign that God's compassion reaches beyond Israel to the Gentile nations.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Jonah 1:1-2 (Nineveh, 'that great city,' whose wickedness has come up before God)",
    "Jonah 3:1-10 (the city's repentance in sackcloth and God's relenting from judgment)",
    "Jonah 4:10-11 (God's declared pity on Nineveh's 120,000 inhabitants)",
    "Matthew 12:41 ('The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment... for they repented at the preaching of Jonah')",
    "Luke 11:30-32 (Jonah a sign to the Ninevites; their repentance contrasted with 'this generation')"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Nineveh as the archetype of the cruel, violent, arrogant pagan empire under God's certain judgment — the 'bloody city' whose destruction demonstrates that no human power escapes divine justice. This is the dominant note in Nahum and Zephaniah and is a fully standard reading alongside the repentance motif.",
      "basis": [
        "Nahum 1:1-8; 2:8-13; 3:1-7 ('Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder')",
        "Zephaniah 2:13-15 (Nineveh made a desolation, the exultant city that said 'I am, and there is no one else')",
        "Genesis 10:11-12 (Nineveh founded in the line of Nimrod, associating it with Assyrian imperial power)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Nineveh as a type or foreshadowing of the Gentile church / the inclusion of the nations in salvation — a reading prominent in patristic and later typological interpretation (e.g., Jerome, Augustine), where the repentant Gentile city prefigures the Gentiles' reception of the gospel while Israel resists.",
      "basis": [
        "Jonah 3 read typologically",
        "Matthew 12:41 / Luke 11:32 (repentant Gentiles contrasted with unbelieving Israel)",
        "Patristic commentary on Jonah (Jerome's Commentary on Jonah; Augustine, City of God 18.44)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Nineveh as a cautionary symbol of the impermanence of repentance: the city that repented under Jonah later returned to wickedness and was destroyed (Nahum), so Nineveh warns that a single generation's repentance does not secure a people permanently.",
      "basis": [
        "Jonah 3 read together with Nahum 1-3",
        "Tobit 14:4, 8-15 (in traditions using the deuterocanon, Nineveh's later destruction confirmed)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Allegorical/patristic readings of Nineveh as 'the world' or the fallen human city more broadly (sometimes contrasted with Jerusalem/the church), with Jonah's mission read as Christ's mission into the world; found in some patristic and medieval spiritual exegesis but not a standard modern reading.",
      "basis": [
        "Allegorical exegesis of Jonah in patristic and medieval commentary (e.g., readings in the tradition of Origen-influenced spiritual interpretation and Jerome)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Nineveh in Augustine's discussion as an occasion for reflecting on prophecy and divine relenting — 'Nineveh was overthrown' understood as fulfilled in its moral overthrow (its old sinful self destroyed by repentance) rather than physical destruction; a specific interpretive move rather than a general symbolic meaning.",
      "basis": [
        "Jonah 3:4 with Jonah 3:10",
        "Augustine, City of God 21.24 and related patristic discussion of conditional prophecy"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Nineveh carries a well-recognized dual symbolism in Christian interpretation, and the two strands are not truly in conflict: (1) the repentant city of Jonah, emblem of God's mercy, the efficacy of repentance, and God's concern for the Gentiles — reinforced by Jesus' explicit appeal to the Ninevites; and (2) the wicked, violent imperial city judged and destroyed in Nahum and Zephaniah, emblem of divine justice against arrogant powers. Sermonic, catechetical, and devotional usage overwhelmingly foregrounds the Jonah/repentance meaning (helped by Jesus' citation), which is why it is listed as primary; academic and canonical-context treatments give the Nahum judgment theme roughly equal weight. Both readings are firmly established; disagreement concerns emphasis, not substance."
}

In the prophetic tradition of Nahum and Zephaniah, it stands as the ultimate tyrannical and bloodthirsty empire destined for divine wrath."
}

      ],

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is no single settled symbolic definition of Nineveh across Christian interpretation. Its canonical portrayals differ: Jonah emphasizes pagan wickedness, repentance, mission, and mercy, while Nahum emphasizes imperial violence and irreversible judgment. The broadest recognizable synthesis is therefore a sinful pagan society accountable to God, capable of repentance, and otherwise subject to judgment."

BOOK ENTRY
A great city of the sea — gentile peoples who repent and rise in judgment.

Matthew 12:41 — The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
